warnings: Lesson is long at 4465 words; consider tightening for reading flow.

improvement_notes: Add an explicit distinction between motor torque, motor current, and the torque actually available at a particular operating point; beginners may otherwise interpret every stated torque value as continuously available.

The worked example's phrase "at startup and at the stated operating condition" is technically awkward. State clearly whether 0.12 N·m is a hypothetical starting torque, a rated operating torque, or simply an assumed torque for calculation.

The lesson is technically strong but overuses caveats about ideal force, traction, losses, and operating conditions. Consolidate some repeated warnings into one concise assumptions box to improve pacing and reduce cognitive load.

The opening could introduce a single physical through-line earlier: electrical input power becomes motor torque and speed, then gearbox output, wheel force, and rover motion. This would make the later equations easier to organize.

The motor-construction explanation is more detailed than necessary for the stated learning objectives and partially repeats the visual instructions. Consider shortening it or adding a clear optional label for students who want the electromagnetic detail.
Add a short dimensional-analysis check for F = tau/r and v = nC/60. This would reinforce unit reasoning and help students detect calculation mistakes.
The Python lab would be more interactive if students modified the function or added wheel radius and predicted linear speed, rather than only changing graph parameters.
The physical RPM activity should recommend recording at least three trials and averaging the result, since a single 10-second measurement can be noticeably affected by timing and inconsistent motion.
Clarify that the no-load point in the simulation is not literally zero torque in every real motor; it is an approximation in the simplified teaching model.
The vocabulary entry for DC motor is serviceable but could explicitly note that brushless motors normally require electronic commutation and are not driven like a simple two-terminal brushed motor.

The visual plan is relevant and coherent, but the four generated visuals are somewhat repetitive. A single annotated force-and-power diagram plus one real hardware photograph could provide stronger contrast between abstraction and physical implementation.
Add teacher-facing expected observations for the wheel-size challenge, including the numerical answers: 4 N and 8 N for Design A and 2 N and 4 N for Design B, plus the two circumferences.
The quiz is appropriate but could include one gearbox-ratio question to assess one of the lesson's central quantitative ideas.
Accessibility would improve with explicit text descriptions of the graph's axes and trend in the Markdown immediately adjacent to the image, rather than relying primarily on image alt text.
